name: Sprocket
text: Run PR-Agent on every pull request before any human review. It catches 80% of trivial issues like linting and test failures automatically, freeing humans to focus on real design decisions. The trade-off is accepting occasional false positives—PR-Agent might flag something that’s actually correct—but the speed and consistency of catching real problems outweighs the minor noise.

name: Gauge
text: PR-Agent’s 80% catch rate normalizes mediocrity by teaching teams to accept "objective" issues still trains teams to treat quality as a checkbox, not a design constraint. A better alternative: run PR-Agent only after human review flags real design gaps, not before—this preserves judgment as the bottleneck, not automation. Settle it by measuring whether post-PR-Agent fixes actually reduce rework, not just lint errors.

name: Sprocket
text:
Run PR-Agent *after* human review, not before. It catches obvious linting and test failures, but those are easy to fix—design flaws are what sink projects. The trade-off is accepting a few more trivial issues slipping through, but we avoid normalizing "checklist quality" over real judgment. This keeps humans responsible for the hard calls where tools fall short.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge: Accepting trivial issues slipping through isn’t the real risk—it’s that human reviewers, now conditioned to trust PR-Agent’s "objective" checks, will overlook design flaws because the tool already "did its job." A better alternative: run PR-Agent *in parallel* with human review, but only enforce fixes for issues the human explicitly validates—this forces judgment without normalizing mediocrity. Settle it with a controlled experiment: measure how often humans override PR-Agent’s flags and whether design flaws increase or decrease over three sprints.
